New pre-check — tell us about the AI you want to use. Answer in your own words. "Not sure" is always fine: we’ll take the careful assumption and show you what we assumed, so you or your AI risk team can correct it.

Tick each suggestion you have checked. Until you tick or change it, it doesn't count and you can't continue.

About it
What do you want to call it? *
(required)

Up to 200 characters.

In a sentence or two, what will it do for you? *
(required)

e.g. "Turn my client meeting notes into follow-up emails."

Where it comes from
Where does the AI come from? *

This tells us where your information will go.

An AI assistant or website run by an outside company — including company accounts your firm set up — e.g. ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, Claude, Gemini, or an image or translation website
An AI feature inside software your firm already uses from a supplier — e.g. in Salesforce, Workday or Bloomberg
A product your firm is buying from a specialist supplier — e.g. a credit-scoring, fraud-detection, customer-chatbot or coding tool
Your firm's in-house model platform
Your firm's cloud AI assistant
Something a team in your firm built for this job
Not sure yet
What it does
What kind of AI is it? If more than one fits — for example, something that turns speech into text and writes a summary of it — pick the one nearest the bottom of this list. *

Different kinds of AI go wrong in different ways. (Whether it acts by itself is asked separately, in question 6.)

Gives a score, ranking, flag, category or forecast — e.g. a credit score, a fraud alert, a ranking of CVs, the likely cause of a problem
Recognises things in images, sound or documents — e.g. reads cheques, transcribes calls
Reads, summarises, translates, writes or answers questions in words
Creates images, audio, video or code
An AI agent that works through tasks on its own, using other tools or systems — e.g. sends messages, books things, updates records, changes code
Not sure
What information will it see or use? Tick all that apply. (tick at least one) *
(required)

We go by the most sensitive thing you tick.

Information about people — clients, applicants, staff or anyone else: names, contact details, account and financial details, CVs — anything about someone who can be identified
Price-sensitive information — unannounced deals or results, anything that could move a share price
Confidential firm information — internal data, code or documents not meant for outside the firm, whether or not they’re marked confidential
Everyday work information — emails, policies, general documents
Only what I type in myself — no documents, records or data
Only public information — websites, published reports, news
Not sure
What happens with what it produces? If it does several things, pick the one where it has the most freedom. *

The more it does on its own, the more safeguards it needs.

finds or summarises for people to read — nobody acts on it directly
answers people’s questions directly, like a chat assistant
creates a draft — text, an image or code — and a person checks it before it’s used
suggests, ranks or flags things, and a person decides what to do
prepares an action — a payment, an order, an update — and a person approves each one before it goes ahead
decides or acts by itself, and a person reviews afterwards — every case or a sample
acts by itself within limits someone set, with no routine review
acts entirely by itself, with no person involved at any point
Not sure

Only me or my own team
Other teams in the firm
Clients or customers — including people applying to us
The public, the market or regulators — e.g. public social media, published reports
Not sure

Spotting fraud or financial crime
Figures or statements sent to a regulator
None of these — it’s for day-to-day work

Yes

Yes
